summary: AgriSAR turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into simple answers. Farmers draw their land, choose a crop, and get a readiness score from 0 to 100, a map of where to plant, and the main limiting factor. The score is based on NISAR soil moisture, water, land state and fire damage, plus ERA5 climate and terrain. Governments and environmental groups use it to detect deforestation, wildfires and excess water every 12 days. NISAR’s L-band radar sees through clouds and vegetation, and the app speaks six languages and Moroccan Darija, so the data reaches the farmers who need it.
details:
AgriSAR: NISAR radar for farmers and land guardians

AgriSAR is a web application that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar data into clear answers for two kinds of users: farmers who ask “Can I plant this crop here, and where?”, and organizations or governments who ask “Is this land being cleared, burned or flooded?”

How it works: the user draws an area on a map and picks a period. AgriSAR finds the NISAR files over that area (GCOV backscatter at 20 m, GUNW coherence at 80 m, SME2 soil moisture at 200 m), downloads only the needed pixels, and analyses them. It shows:

  • the land state (bare soil, crops, forest, water, buildings);
  • events: deforestation, forest loss, wildfire (confirmed with NASA FIRMS), excess water;
  • the fire history over many years;
  • a land-readiness score from 0 to 100 for 16 crops, such as argan, olive and wheat.

The score combines seven factors: soil moisture, excess water, fire, land today, forest clearing, climate (10 years of ERA5) and terrain (slope and altitude). Each is compared with the crop’s needs from FAO EcoCrop and agroforestry databases. The score follows FAO’s “most limiting factor” rule and names the factor that holds it back. A map shows where to plant and where not. A printable report explains every formula with its numbers.

Benefits and impact: L-band radar sees through clouds, at night, and through vegetation, so it works when optical satellites fail. Farmers get advice without a field visit. Organizations can monitor deforestation, fires and flooding every 12 days.

Accessibility: six languages (English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Arabic, Japanese), a simple farmer view and an expert view, and a voice assistant, Nisa, who understands and speaks Moroccan Darija, for farmers who prefer speaking to reading.

Tools:

  • Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, pyproj);
  • JavaScript (React, Vite, MapLibre, satellite.js);
  • Google Gemini for the assistant and the written report;
  • Microsoft Azure Speech for the voice;

No special hardware: ordinary laptops.

Creativity and factors considered:

  • We honestly separate measured facts from rules of thumb.
  • We say “excess water” instead of “flood” when it’s only inferred from radar.
  • We take the EU Deforestation Regulation into account.
  • We keep all keys on the server.
  • We show the limits openly: field size versus pixel size, a 12-day revisit, and weights based on expert judgment, to be refined with agronomists.
